title: Baron Crumbs and the Lost Crown
markdown:
In a very cosy little house lived Baron Crumbs, the mouse king. Being a king is a very big job, and he was quite good at it. His grand castle was a fancy shoebox with a soft velvet cushion for a throne. On his head he always wore his magnificent crown. It was not gold. It was a sparkly bottle cap polished until it gleamed like a tiny disco ball, red and silver stripes winking when the sun hit them just right.

His best friend in the whole wide world was Nettle. Nettle was a small emerald-green newt with eyes like shiny black beads that sparkled with mischief. He loved adventures more than particularly juicy worms, which is saying something. His webbed feet made a splish-splash when he hurried about, which was often.

One sunny morning, the kind where dust motes dance like tiny fairies in the sunbeams, Baron Crumbs woke, stretched his whiskers, and reached for his crown. His paw touched nothing. He patted his fluffy head. Nothing.

“My crown!” he squeaked, tail twitching like a nervous caterpillar. A tremor rippled through his whiskers. The missing crown felt like fizzy lemonade bubbling in his tummy. He often got lost in little worries, especially about his comfort.

Nettle, who had been doing a happy dance on the windowsill, wiggled over. “What’s wrong, Your Majesty?” His voice was a bubbly gurgle, like water over pebbles.

“My crown is gone!” wailed Baron Crumbs, and he let out a mouse-sized sob that sounded like a squeaky door hinge. His ears drooped like wilted flowers.

They searched everywhere. Under the shoebox throne, which was surprisingly cavernous. Behind the crumb collection—a meticulous pile of the finest bread bits and biscuit fragments the Baron had carefully curated. They even looked in Nettle’s favourite puddle-spot by the leaky tap, which smelled of damp earth and adventure. Nothing. Then Nettle spotted a faint trail of flour dust. Tiny white footprints led from the throne toward the mysterious pantry door.

“The pantry,” gasped Nettle, bright green body vibrating. “It must have rolled in there. And the only place with that much flour is the Flour Cave.”

Even saying the name made Nettle’s wiggles go a little wigglier. The pantry was a giant dark land for tiny creatures, full of towering cans like metal skyscrapers and echoing darkness that whispered secrets. The Flour Cave was the deepest dustiest part, where the flour bags slept like enormous white sheep. Things that rolled in there, it was said, sometimes stayed forever, lost in the powdery fluff. The Baron needed his crown back before he got too sad to be king. A sad king is no fun at all, not even for the bravest newts.

Nettle had an idea that popped into his head like a fizzy bubble. He scampered to a shelf where the human kept interesting things and found a tiny shimmering bottle filled with a liquid that smelled like strawberries and fizzy pop. “We’ll shrink,” he declared, eyes shining like dew. “Then we can sneak in and find your crown.”

Baron Crumbs gulped. Shrinking? Into the giant dusty pantry? His whiskers quivered. He looked at the smooth unadorned space where his crown should be, then at Nettle’s determined buzzing face. “All right, Nettle. Let’s do it.”

They each took a tiny sip. It tickled their tongues. Then—whoosh. The world exploded in size. The shoebox castle looked like a mountain range. The floorboards stretched like vast wooden plains. They were no bigger than a ladybug. Baron Crumbs felt as if he were tumbling down a soft fluffy hill.

They tiptoed to the pantry door, a giant brown cliff face. Nettle, being the bravest and wigglest, pushed it open a crack. The sound boomed like thunder. They squeezed through, wriggling like two tiny caterpillars, one green and one brown.

Inside was a colossal echoing cave. Jars of jam loomed like colourful glassy planets, sticky sweetness hanging in the air. A vast sleeping bag of sugar. And then the smell: the dusty powdery smell of the Flour Cave, like a million sleepy clouds.

“This way,” whispered Nettle, leading through a landscape of fallen rice grains that crunched like hailstones. They entered the soft white dust. It was like walking through a cloud. The flour tickled their noses and got in their whiskers. Baron Crumbs sneezed so hard he disappeared in a puff of white, then reappeared looking like a little ghost.

Nettle froze mid-wiggle. “Look.” There, on a small snowy hill of flour, sat the sparkly bottle-cap crown. It glinted even in the dim light.

Baron Crumbs scurried toward it—and then his eyes gleamed with a different light. Nestled right beside the crown was a tiny forgotten biscuit crumb, deliciously crumbly and sweet. “Ooooh, a biscuit,” he mumbled, kingly duties a distant memory. He started to nibble, whiskers already dusted white, completely lost in the taste.

“Baron,” Nettle squeaked, a tiny bell in the dusty silence. “We need to go. It isn’t safe. The cat might come.”

Baron Crumbs looked up, mouth full. He saw the giant jars and the dark corners and remembered how scared he had been to come in. He also saw the biscuit. He could stay here in the quiet dusty cave and just be lazy and eat. He faltered.

Then he looked at Nettle—his brave wiggly friend who had shrunk down and come all this way, just for him. Nettle was not tempted by forgotten crumbs. He was thinking about getting them both home.

A thought as clear as a dewdrop popped into the Baron’s head. Being king was not only about having a crown. It was about being brave for your friends. It was about remembering what mattered. He spat out the biscuit crumb. “You’re right, Nettle. My crown. And then home.”

Just as they reached for the crown, a giant shadow fell over them. A huge fuzzy orange thing was stirring in the darkness. Bartholomew the house cat had come to investigate the strange exciting smell of shrinking potion and tiny mice. His padded paw, claws surprisingly sharp, was coming down right for them.

They had to act now. Nettle grabbed the crown with all his might, little green arms straining. Baron Crumbs saw the paw descend, large and soft, and Bartholomew’s warm fur smelling faintly of sunshine and dust. He knew the perfect golden biscuit crumb he had saved for last, right beside the crown, was in danger. With a desperate squeak he pushed the crown, sending it skittering across the flour, deliberately nudging it away from the crumb. The paw landed with a soft thud, crushing the precious biscuit, its sweet scent lost in the dust. Air whooshed as the paw swept past.

“Hold on tight,” Nettle shouted. He gave the crown a mighty wiggle and a push. It skittered like a runaway hockey puck. They scrambled after it, the cat’s enormous whiskers tickling their backs like giant feathery dusters. The smell of cat was overwhelming, warm and dusty, making their tiny noses twitch.

They reached the pantry’s edge and, with a final desperate heave, pushed the crown through the gap in the door. It landed safely on the floorboards.

Bartholomew’s nose twitched. He yawned a giant pink yawn that showed formidable teeth, lost interest in the dusty empty space, and padded away, tail swishing lazily. They scampered out, the sparkly crown between them, and sat by the leaky tap, green and brown bodies covered in a fine layer of white powder. They drank the rest of the shrinking potion. Whoosh. They were back to their usual sizes, right in time for afternoon tea. Their clothes, which had shrunk with them, popped back too.

Baron Crumbs placed his crown on his head. It felt heavier now, not because it was gold, but because of the adventure they had shared. He looked at Nettle, eyes beaming like polished buttons.

“Thank you, my dear Nettle. You were the bravest wigglest friend a king could ever have. I couldn’t have done it without you.”

Nettle’s wiggles returned in full force. “And you, Your Majesty, were a very brave king who remembered what was important. More important than biscuits, even.”

From that day on Baron Crumbs always made sure his crown was extra secure, maybe with a little sticky honey on the inside so it would not slip. More importantly, he remembered that the best adventures, and the best crowns, are those shared with a true friend. And sometimes he even shared a biscuit crumb with Nettle, just for old times’ sake.
